idiom_name: struct records in arrays walked through Span<T> / CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan
implementation_notes: The layout is built from value types plus the System.Memory primitives rather than from any framework role: define records as structs (no object header, no boxing), keep them in T[] or List<T>, and walk them through Span<T> - 'a type-safe and memory-safe representation of a contiguous region of arbitrary memory' that can point at managed arrays, native memory or the stack (learn.microsoft.com). CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list) hands out a span over a List<T>'s backing array without copying (net-5.0+), which is the replacement for traversing a graph of objects; because Span<T> is a stack-only ref struct it cannot be stored in a field or survive await/yield, so the array owns the storage and only the view travels. Use ArrayPool<T>.Shared for large transient buffers (rent/return) and one array or span per column for struct-of-arrays layouts; the segmented per-column list is the classic structure that the span view supersedes.
pitfalls: A struct with a reference field (string, object, another class) or a class record reintroduces the pointer chase and stops being blittable - keep hot records as unmanaged value types.
CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan is only valid while the list's structure is unchanged; adding or removing elements while the span is live reads freed or stale storage.
Span<T> cannot be boxed, used as a field, or cross await/yield boundaries; use Memory<T> when the view must live on the heap, and re-create the span per operation.
Rented arrays are not zeroed on return and are larger than requested: always slice to the exact count (pool.AsSpan(0, count)) and return them in a finally block.
